Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is among the deadliest solid tumors, with a five-year relative survival rate of approximately 13% [@siegel2026cancer] and limited responsiveness to existing therapies. A decade of bulk-transcriptomic effort has produced robust tumor-intrinsic subtypes (Basal-like and Classical [@collisson2011subtypes; @moffitt2015virtual; @rashid2020purity]) and stromal subtypes (tumor-promoting proCAF and tumor-restraining restCAF [@peng2024determination]), each of which is single-sample deployable and validated across cohorts. Whether the joint configuration of these tumor and stromal compartments carries prognostic information beyond what the discrete subtypes capture individually, and whether such an integrated axis can be recovered de novo from bulk transcriptomes, remains incompletely understood. Identifying the transcriptional programs that predict clinical outcomes is central to molecular subtyping and prognostic stratification in cancer. While single-cell and spatial technologies clarify the cellular states present in tumors [@chansengyue2020transcription; @werba2023single], bulk transcriptomic profiling remains the primary platform for cohort-scale survival annotation and prognostic modeling in large clinical cohorts [@bair2004semi; @aung2018compass]. Each expression profile is a composite of malignant cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), immune infiltrates, and other microenvironmental components [@nguyen2024fourteen]. As a result, these signatures may be diluted or obscured by variation in cellular composition across samples. Nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) has been instrumental in resolving this mixture into additive, interpretable gene programs corresponding to recognizable cell types or transcriptional states [@lee1999learning; @moffitt2015virtual; @peng2019novo]. In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), this approach has yielded key biological insights, including the identification of molecular subtypes [@collisson2011subtypes; @Bailey2016; @rashid2020purity; @peng2024determination], the Basal-like and Classical tumor programs defined through virtual microdissection [@moffitt2015virtual], and compartment-specific deconvolution of tumor and microenvironmental signals [@peng2019novo].

However, the standard approach discovers these programs through unsupervised factorization [@brunet2004metagenes] and only then evaluates their clinical relevance retrospectively [@Bailey2016; @collisson2011subtypes]. Because unsupervised NMF minimizes reconstruction error, its factors tend to be dominated by the highest-variance patterns in the data, which may reflect tissue composition or other outcome-neutral sources rather than prognostic biology [@bair2004semi; @cook2007fisher]. In PDAC, tissue-composition signals such as from exocrine cells reflect low tumor purity rather than cancer cell-intrinsic programs and carry little prognostic value [@rashid2020purity; @peng2024determination]. This misalignment between variance and prognosis extends beyond PDAC: tumor purity alone accounts for a large fraction of expression variation across cancer types [@aran2015systematic], yet the objective optimized during unsupervised discovery (reconstruction error) differs fundamentally from the criterion used during evaluation (survival association) [@cook2007fisher]. Reconstruction alone also leaves the factor basis non-identifiable [@donoho2004nmf; @laurberg2008uniqueness; @gillis2014nmf], contributing to the cross-study variability observed among unsupervised cancer subtype taxonomies. Identifying the prognostically relevant programs among the discovered factors requires extensive downstream evaluation: over a decade of PDAC subtyping was needed to converge on a robust Basal-like/Classical dichotomy, first defined through virtual microdissection [@moffitt2015virtual] and subsequently confirmed in independent cohorts [@rashid2020purity], single-cell analyses [@chansengyue2020transcription; @werba2023single], and prospective clinical profiling [@aung2018compass].

This raises a concrete biological question: which transcriptional programs carry stable prognostic information across PDAC cohorts, and how are they distributed across the tumor and stromal compartments that bulk transcriptomes mix together? We address this through two non-circular tests: recovery of ground-truth program identities in simulations where the true gene sets are known a priori, and out-of-sample generalization to five independent PDAC cohorts on which no model parameters were estimated.

Here we present DeSurv, a survival-supervised deconvolution framework that integrates nonnegative matrix factorization with Cox proportional hazards modeling so that gene programs are shaped during discovery by both reconstruction and survival. The supervision is routed onto the gene-program matrix while preserving the mixture-coefficient interpretation of sample loadings, and the trained gene programs score new samples by simple projection without retraining (Methods).

We evaluate DeSurv in two settings. In simulations with known latent structure and survival associations, DeSurv recovers the true factorization rank and prognostic programs more reliably than standard NMF. Critically, its advantage scales with the gap between the highest-variance and most prognostic subspaces and vanishes under null conditions where no survival signal exists, confirming that the method adapts to the structure of the data rather than imposing spurious survival associations. In PDAC, survival supervision produces a different factor structure: DeSurv concentrates survival signal into a single factor coupling Classical tumor identity with tumor-restraining CAF (restCAF)-associated stroma, a prognostic axis that unsupervised methods distribute across multiple factors, while the exocrine-compositional variation that dominates standard NMF is not represented as a dedicated factor. These survival-aligned factors generalize to five independent PDAC cohorts without retraining, with stronger out-of-sample survival stratification than their unsupervised counterparts. Because the misalignment between reconstruction-optimal and outcome-relevant subspaces is not unique to PDAC (tumor purity variation dominates expression landscapes across cancer types), DeSurv provides a general framework for extracting outcome-relevant programs from bulk tumor transcriptomes wherever unsupervised factors conflate biological signal with compositional noise. Survival-supervised cross-validation provides an outcome-informed criterion for rank selection, offering a route to generalizable prognostic biomarkers and biological insight into tumor--stroma coupling in cancers like PDAC where compositional variation dominates expression. The method is implemented in an open-source R package (https://github.com/rashidlab/DeSurv).
